section.title: Vindicate Me, O Lord
section.sectionRationale: A psalm of integrity, in which David asks the LORD to examine his heart and vindicate him against false accusation, grounding his confidence not in sinless perfection but in sincere trust, love for God's house, and deliberate separation from deceit and violence.
section.thesis: David asks the LORD to test his heart and vindicate him, resting his confidence not on flawless performance but on sincere covenant loyalty, love for God's presence in worship, and a settled resolve to walk apart from the wicked.
section.frameNote: Four movements: a plea for vindication rooted in integrity and trust (1-3); deliberate separation from evildoers alongside love for God's house and worship (4-8); a prayer not to be swept away with sinners (9-10); and a renewed resolve to walk in integrity, closing with redemption and blessing in the congregation (11-12).

units.label: Vindicate me, O LORD
units.note: a plea rooted in integrity and trust

verses.text:
Vindicate me, O LORD! 
For I have walked with {{tom|integrity}}; I have trusted in the LORD without wavering.
{{bachan|Test}} me, O LORD, and try me; examine my heart and mind.
For Your {{chesed|loving devotion}} is before my eyes, and I have walked in Your truth.

units.label: I love the house where You dwell
units.note: separation from evildoers, love for worship

verses.text: I do not sit with deceitful men, nor keep company with hypocrites.
I hate the mob of evildoers, and refuse to sit with the wicked.
I wash my hands in innocence that I may go about Your altar, O LORD,
to raise my voice in thanksgiving and declare all Your wonderful works.
O LORD, I love the house where You dwell, the place where Your glory resides.

units.label: Do not take my soul away with sinners
units.note: a prayer for separation from judgment

verses.text: Do not take my soul away with sinners, or my life with men of bloodshed,
in whose hands are wicked schemes, whose right hands are full of bribes.

units.label: My foot stands on level ground

verses.text: But I will walk with integrity; redeem me and be merciful to me.
My feet stand on level ground; in the congregations I will bless the LORD.

tom.gloss: Integrity, blamelessness, completeness of character. It does not claim sinless perfection but sincere, whole-hearted covenant loyalty, a settled direction of life rather than a flawless record.

bachan.gloss: To test, try, examine, often used of refining metal. David invites God's own scrutiny of his heart rather than avoiding it, confident that sincere trust, not self-deception, will be found there.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion. David keeps God's chesed continually before his eyes, the compass by which he has walked in truth rather than deceit.

basic.context: David asks the LORD to examine him and vindicate him against apparent accusation, grounding his plea not in sinless perfection but in sincere trust, deliberate separation from deceitful and violent men, and genuine love for God's house and worship. The psalm turns from testimony of a well-ordered life to prayer that God would not sweep him away with the wicked, closing with renewed resolve and praise in the assembly.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm should not be read as a claim to sinlessness but as an expression of sincere covenant loyalty, the kind commended throughout Scripture as genuine faith working itself out in a whole-hearted, examined life, not flawless performance but settled direction.
basic.originalLanguages: David's tom, integrity, is not perfection but wholehearted loyalty, tested, bachan, by God's own examination, and grounded in chesed, God's steadfast covenant loving devotion, kept continually before his eyes as the standard by which he has walked.
basic.typology: David's washing of hands in innocence before approaching God's altar, verse 6, anticipates the greater cleansing believers receive in Christ, whose blood allows sinners to draw near to God 'with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience,' Hebrews 10:22.
basic.christ: David's plea to be vindicated points forward to Jesus, the only truly innocent man, whose integrity was vindicated fully and finally by His resurrection, 1 Timothy 3:16. Where David could only wash his hands symbolically before the altar, Christ's own blood accomplishes the real cleansing that lets sinners draw near to God with a clean conscience, Hebrews 10:22, and His zeal for His Father's house, John 2:17, echoes and surpasses David's love for the place where God's glory dwells.
basic.god: God is shown as one who welcomes honest self-examination rather than pretense, inviting His people to bring their hearts under His testing scrutiny, and who is worthy of love expressed in worship at the place where His glory dwells.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Timothy 3:16 shows Christ vindicated by the Spirit, the ultimate answer to David's plea for vindication. Hebrews 10:22 describes hearts sprinkled clean and bodies washed, fulfilling the symbolic hand washing of verse 6. John 2:17 shows Jesus consumed with zeal for His Father's house, echoing David's love for God's dwelling place.
basic.oneStory: David's plea to be examined, vindicated, and welcomed near God's altar despite his need for mercy finds its full answer in Jesus Christ, the only truly innocent one, vindicated by resurrection, whose blood cleanses sinners so they may draw near to God with a clean conscience and genuine, unashamed worship.

context.literary:
The psalm is built on the verb walk. David has walked in integrity, verse 1, and has walked in God's truth, verse 3; he will not sit with the deceitful, verse 4, and he ends by resolving to walk in integrity again, verse 11. The opening claim and the closing vow share the same phrase, so the whole prayer is wrapped in one sentence about a life. Between the two the psalm moves inward and then outward: the first section is addressed to God alone (verses 1 to 3), the middle sections describe two kinds of company, the assembly of the wicked and the place where God's glory dwells (verses 4 to 10), and the last verse lands in the public gathering, where the private plea becomes a public blessing.

Notice how the imagery of assembly frames the piece. In verse 5 David refuses the company of evildoers, and the noun there is a gathering, the same family of word that gives the plural 'congregations' in verse 12. Two rival assemblies compete for his presence, and the psalm ends by saying which one he will bless the LORD in. The altar in verse 6 sits at the exact centre of the poem, and the love of the dwelling place in verse 8 is its peak, so the request for judgment is built around worship rather than around the accusers.

The style is legal as well as devotional. David opens with a request for a verdict, verse 1, offers evidence in verses 4 to 8, and pleads for a favourable sentence in verses 9 to 11. Three verbs of examination in verse 2 (test, try, examine) sound like a cross examination that the accused himself invites. Then, unlike the prayers of Psalm 25 that came just before it, which leaned on God's forgiveness of sin, this psalm places its weight on what God has seen in the walk. The two psalms are meant to be prayed as a pair: one begging pardon, one resting in a life that pardon has made possible.
context.historical:
Ancient Israel had no police force or professional courts in the modern sense. Serious disputes were settled by elders at the gate, and when there was no witness the matter could be taken before God himself, at his sanctuary. Exodus 22:9 speaks of a case that 'shall come before God', and Solomon's dedication prayer pictures a man taking an oath before the altar, asking God to condemn the guilty and justify the righteous, 1 Kings 8:31 to 32. Many readers hear Psalm 26 in that setting: a person under suspicion who has come to the altar and asks the LORD, not the crowd, to give the verdict.

The washing of the hands in verse 6 draws on a real rite. When a body was found in open country and the killer was unknown, the elders of the nearest town washed their hands over a heifer and declared, 'Our hands did not shed this blood,' Deuteronomy 21:6 to 7. The gesture was a public statement of innocence. The psalmist takes that outward custom and turns it into a prayer, using the word 'innocence' for the condition of the hands. The priests had a separate washing before they served at the altar, Exodus 30:19 to 21, and David combines the two ideas: innocent hands, and the privilege of going about God's altar.

The setting for a king is worth stating. A ruler surrounded by officials could be accused by hidden rivals, and the 'bribes' in verse 10 belonged to that world, where a judge's right hand could be bought. David's prayer about the men whose hands are full of bribes is the sharpest contrast with his own washed hands. The 'house' of verse 8 was, in his day, the tent that held the ark, and its glory was the visible sign that God was present with Israel, Exodus 40:34 to 35. The psalmist loves a place because he loves the God who has chosen to be there.
context.canonical:
Psalm 26 sits in a run of prayers in which David asks to be judged by God: Psalm 7:8 says 'vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity,' Psalm 17:3 says 'You have tried my heart... You have tested me and found no evil,' and Psalm 18:20 says the LORD has rewarded him according to the cleanness of his hands. These psalms have to be read with Psalm 32:5, where the same man says 'I acknowledged my sin to You,' and with Psalm 143:2, 'no one alive is righteous before You.' The Psalter never allows a claim to integrity to stand alone. It is set beside confession so that the reader learns that the two belong together.

Psalm 24:3 to 4 asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and answers, 'He who has clean hands and a pure heart.' Psalm 26 is the prayer of a person trying to live up to that entrance liturgy, and Psalm 24 in turn ends by welcoming the King of glory to His gates. The book also opens with the same shape, Psalm 1:1 describing the blessed person as one who does not walk with the wicked or sit with mockers, and Psalm 26 makes that first psalm personal.

In the New Testament the hand washing of verse 6 is taken up at the cross, where Pilate washes his hands and declares himself innocent of this man's blood, Matthew 27:24, an inversion of the psalm: a man claiming clean hands while condemning the only innocent one. The early believers lift up holy hands in prayer, 1 Timothy 2:8, and the letter to the Hebrews invites people to draw near with sprinkled hearts, Hebrews 10:22. Paul can speak of a clear conscience, 2 Corinthians 1:12, without denying his need of grace.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David wants his hearers to see that a claim to integrity is not arrogance if it is offered to God and not to the crowd. He does not stand in the street and defend himself; he goes to the altar and asks the one Judge who can see the heart to look. That is the first thing the psalm teaches: that innocence before people and honesty before God are two different tests, and that the second is the one that counts.

He also means to show what integrity looks like in practice. It is not vague goodness. It is a set of choices about company, verses 4 and 5, about worship, verses 6 to 8, and about money and influence, verse 10. The believer chooses which gathering to sit in, and the choosing shapes the person.

At the same time the psalm is not a boast that the speaker has arrived. The request that God 'redeem' him, verse 11, and the fear that he might be swept away with sinners, verse 9, show a man who knows he could be taken along with the wrong crowd. The first hearers were meant to learn a settled direction: love the place where God dwells, refuse the company that mocks Him, and ask for mercy in the same breath as justice.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm records David's own testimony and prayer. It does not command every reader to claim what David claims, and a believer who copies verse 1 word for word without David's circumstances may end up saying something untrue. The New Testament is blunt that anyone who says he has no sin deceives himself, 1 John 1:8. What carries over is the pattern rather than the wording: invite God to test the heart, choose your company carefully, love public worship, and rest on mercy.

The hatred of verse 5 is a description of a moral stand, not a licence for personal contempt. The psalmist refuses the assembly of the wicked; he does not ask to harm anyone. Psalm 139:21 to 22 shows the same language, and it is immediately followed by a request that God search the heart, verses 23 and 24. Jesus later commands love for enemies, Matthew 5:44, so a Christian reads verse 5 as separation from wickedness, not from wicked people who need the gospel.

Finally, the psalm does not say that separation earns God's favour. The prayer ends with a request for redemption, so the walk is the fruit of trust, verse 1, not the ground of it.

debates.question: Is David claiming to be sinless when he says he has walked in integrity, verses 1 and 11?

views.label: He claims real but imperfect integrity, a settled loyalty to the LORD
views.case: The psalm ends with a request to be redeemed and treated with mercy, verse 11, which makes no sense from a man who thought he needed no grace. The Hebrew word for integrity means wholeness and undividedness, not flawlessness, and David elsewhere confesses sin, Psalm 32:5.

views.label: He speaks only about the charge laid against him, not about his whole life
views.case: Because the setting looks legal, verse 1 may answer one accusation, as Psalm 7:8 does. On this reading David says he is innocent of the crime he is charged with, and he leaves his general condition in God's hands, Psalm 143:2.

views.label: The psalm should be prayed with caution and balanced by the psalms of confession
views.case: A reader who takes the words at face value could slide into self-righteousness. The Psalter keeps Psalm 26 beside Psalm 25 and 32, teaching that integrity and confession belong together.

debates.bearing: On every reading David appeals to mercy while testifying to sincerity. The lesson for a believer is not to imitate the claim but to keep the two prayers, 'test me' and 'redeem me', in the same breath.

debates.question: What is the setting of the psalm: a legal appeal at the sanctuary or a general prayer of worship?

views.label: A person accused at the altar asks God for a verdict
views.case: The request for vindication in verse 1, the hand washing in verse 6, the fear of being 'taken away with sinners' in verse 9 and the language of bribery in verse 10 all suit a court. 1 Kings 8:31 to 32 shows that oaths were sworn before the altar and that God was asked to judge.

views.label: A general prayer of a worshipper who loves the house of God
views.case: Nothing in the psalm names a particular charge or accuser. It could be a prayer for an ordinary pilgrim who wants the LORD to approve his walk, in the manner of Psalm 24:3 to 4, and the concluding blessing in the congregation would then be a normal worship practice.

debates.bearing: Either way the direction of the prayer is the same: the psalmist places his case in the presence of God rather than taking matters into his own hands, and he expects the verdict to be given in worship.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb of examination in verse 2 is worth slowing down for, because David piles up three in a row. 'Test' is bachan, which the basic level has already named; the next two are nasah, 'try', and tsaraph, 'examine', which is the smelter's word for melting down metal to remove the dross. He asks to be put through the furnace. The object of the examination is 'my heart and mind', but the Hebrew of the second word is literally 'my kidneys', as the BSB footnote says. The kidneys were seen as the seat of the deepest and most hidden feelings, so the phrase covers the whole interior from the seat of will to the seat of emotion.

'Vindicate me' in verse 1 is the ordinary Hebrew verb shaphat, 'judge'. There is no separate word for 'vindicate'. David asks to be judged, confident of the result, the same request as Psalm 7:8. The English word 'vindicate' is a fair translation only because David expects the judgment to go in his favour.

The word rendered 'hypocrites' in verse 4 is a participle from the root alam, 'to hide or conceal', so it means something closer to 'those who conceal themselves'. David refuses the company of people who hide what they are. That fits the theme of examination: he asks to be seen, and he refuses those who cannot bear it. The word 'assembly' in verse 5 is qahal, the ordinary word for a gathering of the people, and verse 12 uses a related plural, makhelot, for the 'congregations' in which he will bless the LORD. The wicked also have their assembly, and the psalmist's love is for another.

In verse 8 the 'place where Your glory resides' is mishkan, the very word for the tabernacle, from the verb shakan, 'to dwell'. The same root later gives the Jewish term shekinah, the dwelling presence. David loves the tent because it is where God's glory settled, Exodus 40:34 to 35.

In verse 11 'redeem' is padah, 'to ransom or buy back', the verb used for the redeeming of a firstborn son and of Israel from Egypt, Deuteronomy 7:8. It sits beside a second verb, chanan, 'be gracious', which is the verb behind 'merciful'. Notice that the man who has just described his integrity asks for a ransom. Finally, the 'level ground' of verse 12 is mishor, a flat, straight place where feet do not stumble, and the same word appears in Psalm 27:11, 'lead me on a level path.' The two psalms have been placed side by side.

typology.type: The washed hands and the altar, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: David combines the innocent washing of Deuteronomy 21:6 to 7 with the priestly washing that let a man approach the altar, Exodus 30:19 to 21. In the New Testament the washing is fulfilled in a way that David could only picture. Believers draw near 'with a sincere heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience and our bodies washed with pure water,' Hebrews 10:22, and the cleansing is by the blood of Christ, not by anything the worshipper does. The correspondence falls short at the point of origin: David washed his own hands, but the New Testament washing is done for the believer, Titus 3:5.

typology.type: Do not take my soul away with sinners, verse 9
typology.fulfillment: David fears being swept off with the wicked in a judgment that does not distinguish. In the story of Christ the direction of this fear is reversed. Jesus, who alone had clean hands and a pure heart, was 'numbered with the transgressors', Isaiah 53:12, quoted in Luke 22:37, and He was crucified between two criminals, Luke 23:33. He was taken away with sinners so that those who trust Him would not be. The type falls short because David asked to be spared; Christ went willingly, John 10:18.

The word padah pictures the ransom of a life. Peter says that believers were redeemed 'not with perishable things such as silver or gold' but with the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18 to 19, and Paul writes that in Christ 'we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses,' Ephesians 1:7. David's prayer is answered at greater cost than he could have guessed. The type is incomplete because David could not name the price; the New Testament does.

typology.type: A foot on level ground, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: The level place is the picture of security after the peril of slander and judgment. The letter to the Hebrews urges believers to 'make straight paths for your feet', Hebrews 12:13, and says that Christ is the one who has gone before, the pioneer of faith, Hebrews 12:2. Isaiah's promise that crooked places will be made straight and rough ground made level, Isaiah 40:4, is fulfilled in the coming of the Lord. The image falls short if pressed literally: the believer's path stays difficult, but the ground beneath it is secure in Christ.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by contrast and then by fulfilment. The contrast is sharpest at the trial. David asked God to test him and find him blameless; Jesus was tested by every court that met Him and was found without fault, Luke 23:4, John 19:4. Pilate washed his hands and said 'I am innocent of this man's blood,' Matthew 27:24, using the very gesture of verse 6 while condemning the only person who could truly have prayed verse 1. What the psalmist claimed with hope, the Son of God possessed in full.

The fulfilment is that the innocence of Jesus is given to those who do not have it. The prayer of verse 11, 'redeem me and be merciful to me,' is answered in His blood, and Paul says that He was made 'to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. The believer who prays this psalm does not claim clean hands of his own. He stands in the clean hands of another, and yet the walk that flows from that standing is still real, Ephesians 2:10, so the psalm remains a pattern for how the redeemed live.

The love for the house of verse 8 is also fulfilled in Christ's own zeal. When He cleansed the temple, His disciples remembered the words, 'Zeal for Your house will consume Me,' John 2:17, quoting Psalm 69:9. David loved the tent of God's glory; Jesus is that glory tabernacling among people, John 1:14, and in His own body the temple is raised, John 2:19 to 21. The love of a place turns into the love of a Person.

The psalm also anticipates the Christian assembly. David resolves to bless the LORD 'in the congregations,' verse 12, and the ascended Christ declares, 'I will proclaim Your name to My brothers; I will sing Your praises in the assembly,' Hebrews 2:12, quoting Psalm 22:22. The one who stands in the assembly is not only David but Christ himself, and He leads the praise of His people.

A caution keeps the reading honest. Not every line applies to Jesus; the prayer for redemption in verse 11 cannot be put on His lips, since He needed no ransom. The psalm speaks of Christ in the way it shapes the longing for a righteous Man, and the New Testament makes the connection, not a fanciful reading of the details.
study.god:
The psalm shows a God who can be examined. David does not ask for a gentle glance; he asks God to test, try and refine his heart, and he can do so because he knows that God's scrutiny is not cruel. God is the one who sees the heart, and that vision is a safety for the righteous and a threat for the hypocrite. The God of Psalm 26 is neither indifferent to sin nor eager to condemn; He judges rightly, and so those who are trusting can ask Him to judge.

He is a God whose loving devotion goes before His people. 'Your loving devotion is before my eyes,' verse 3, means that David walks with God's character as a standard and a comfort. The order matters: God's chesed comes first, and David's walk follows. God's faithful love is the ground; integrity is the response.

He is a God who chooses to dwell. The 'place where Your glory resides,' verse 8, was a tent among the tribes. Israel's God is not remote or confined, and yet He has bound Himself to a place where He may be found. This is the doctrine of God's nearness held together with His transcendence, and it explains why David loves a building: he loves it as the place where the living God has promised to meet him, Exodus 25:22.

He is a God who separates. The psalm has David refuse the company of deceitful people and pray not to be taken away with sinners, and that shows that God is holy and that the righteous and the wicked are not the same in His sight. Yet He also redeems. Verse 11 asks for a ransom, and God's holiness and His willingness to buy back sit next to each other without embarrassment.

He is a God who is honoured with public praise. The psalm ends in congregations, not in a private glow. The worshipper's testimony, verse 7, 'declare all Your wonderful works,' means that God's works are meant to be told. For worship this means that we come with a clean heart, with honesty, and with a wish to be seen; that we choose our company and our gatherings with care; and that we rest our security in the God who redeems and not in our own record.

crossReferences.note: The same request in David's mouth: 'vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity.' Comparing the two shows that the appeal to integrity is a recurring form of prayer in David's life, offered in the face of accusation and always to God as the judge.

'You have tried my heart... You have tested me and found no evil.' Here David reports the result of the testing that Psalm 26:2 asks for. The two verses share the vocabulary of examination and show that David expected God's probing to end in favour of the sincere.

David says the LORD has rewarded him according to the cleanness of his hands. The clean hands of Psalm 26:6 reappear as the ground of reward in a psalm of thanksgiving, which reads best when the confession of Psalm 51 is kept in view.

'He who has clean hands and a pure heart' may ascend the hill of the LORD. Psalm 26 is the prayer of someone who wants to qualify, and the pair show that the entrance to God's presence is a matter of both hands and heart.

'Search me, O God, and know my heart; test me.' The invitation to be examined is repeated in another psalm, and the surrounding verses in Psalm 139:21 to 22 use the language of hatred of evil as Psalm 26:5 does, followed at once by the request that God check whether the speaker himself is at fault.

The elders wash their hands over the heifer and declare their innocence of bloodshed. It is the ritual background to the washing in Psalm 26:6, and it shows that the gesture belongs to a community concerned with atonement, not only to a private claim of purity.

Solomon asks God to hear the oath sworn before the altar, condemning the guilty and justifying the righteous. It supplies a plausible setting for Psalm 26 and shows how the temple functioned as a court of last resort when human evidence ran out.

The blessed man does not walk with the wicked, stand on the path of sinners, or sit with mockers. Psalm 26:4 to 5 puts the same refusal in the first person, 'I do not sit with deceitful men,' and turns the opening picture of the Psalter into a personal vow.

'If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.' It is the necessary counterweight to reading verse 1 as a boast. The apostle allows the confident walk of the believer and blocks the claim of sinlessness, and the psalm's own plea for mercy in verse 11 sits comfortably between them.

Pilate washes his hands and says 'I am innocent of this man's blood.' The ritual of Psalm 26:6 is used by a man who is guilty of the worst injustice, which tells us that clean hands can only be established by God's testing, not by a gesture.

Believers draw near with hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience. The language of washing for the approach to God is carried from the sanctuary into the life of the church, where the cleansing is real and not merely symbolic.

'Zeal for Your house will consume Me.' The disciples see in Jesus the love for God's dwelling that David expresses in Psalm 26:8, quoting Psalm 69:9, and the love is now put into action in the cleansing of the temple.

study.oneStory:
The psalm sits in the middle of the story of how a holy God lives among a sinful people. In Eden the man and woman walked with God in the garden in the cool of the day, Genesis 3:8, and were driven out. Ever since, the Bible has been the story of how to walk with God again. Psalm 26 belongs to the time when the way back was a tent, an altar and a set of washings, and it shows a person who longs to walk that path and who knows he needs to be judged rightly to do so.

The psalm also anticipates the great problem the rest of the story will have to solve. It asks for vindication, and it asks for redemption, and those two requests do not fit together on the ground of the law alone: if God only judged, no one could stand, Psalm 143:2, and if God only forgave without making things right, His justice would be a fiction. The prophets look ahead to a righteous servant who will justify many, Isaiah 53:11, and the psalm's dual request finds its solution in the cross, where God is shown to be 'just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus', Romans 3:26.

The love of the house points along the same line. The tent gives way to the temple, the temple to the body of Christ, and the body of Christ to a people who are built up as a dwelling place for God, Ephesians 2:21 to 22. The congregations of verse 12 are the first hint of the church that will bless the LORD in every nation.

The story ends with a city in which there is no temple, because 'the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple,' Revelation 21:22. The one who longed to go about the altar will not need an altar, because the Lamb is there. The wicked assembly that David refused is gone, because nothing impure will ever enter, Revelation 21:27, and the level ground he prayed for is the street of that city, the ground on which the redeemed finally stand without fear of being swept away.

quiz.q: What does David ask God to do in verse 2?

options.text: Test him, try him, and examine his heart and mind.
options.note: David invites God's own scrutiny rather than avoiding examination.

options.text: Destroy his enemies without delay.
options.note: Verse 2 is a request for self-examination, not for the destruction of enemies.

options.text: Watch him closely without necessarily probing his inner motives.
options.note: Close, since it involves God's attention, but the verb 'examine' specifically targets heart and mind, inner motive, not mere outward observation.

options.text: Remove him from public life.
options.note: David is not asking to withdraw from public life but to be honestly examined by God.

quiz.q: What does David say he does in verses 4-5 regarding deceitful and wicked people?

options.text: He deliberately avoids their company and refuses to sit with them.
options.note: David describes intentional separation from deceitful men, hypocrites, and evildoers.

options.text: He seeks them out to try to reform them.
options.note: The text describes avoidance, not active outreach to reform them.

options.text: He joins them for the sake of influence.
options.note: This is the opposite of David's stated practice of refusing to sit with them.

options.text: He ignores their existence entirely.
options.note: David does more than ignore them; he actively hates their assembly and refuses to associate with them.

quiz.q: What does David say he loves in verse 8?

options.text: The house where the LORD dwells, the place where His glory resides.
options.note: David expresses deep affection for God's dwelling place and the worship that happens there.

options.text: His own royal palace.
options.note: The verse specifically names God's house, not David's palace.

options.text: Worship in general, wherever it happens to occur.
options.note: Close, since worship is in view, but verse 8 specifically names 'the house where You dwell,' a particular place, not worship in the abstract.

options.text: The praise of the people.
options.note: The focus of verse 8 is God's house and glory, not popular acclaim.

quiz.q: What does David ask God not to do in verse 9?

options.text: Take his soul away with sinners or his life with men of bloodshed.
options.note: David asks not to share the fate of the wicked and violent, having deliberately separated from them in life.

options.text: Forget his family after his death.
options.note: The plea concerns not sharing judgment with sinners, not the memory of his family.

options.text: Judge him more severely than the wicked.
options.note: Close, since judgment is the theme, but the verse asks not to be grouped with sinners in judgment, not for a harsher personal sentence.

options.text: Remove him from the throne.
options.note: There is no mention of the throne in this verse; it concerns final judgment with the wicked, not political removal.

quiz.q: How does the psalm end in verse 12?

options.text: With David standing on level ground, resolving to bless the LORD in the congregations.
options.note: The psalm closes with confidence and a resolve to praise God publicly among God's people.

options.text: With David still uncertain of God's favor.
options.note: The psalm closes with settled confidence, not uncertainty, though the psalm as a whole did include real distress earlier.

options.text: With David privately content but silent before others.
options.note: Close, since inner confidence is present, but verse 12 specifically resolves to bless the LORD publicly in the congregations, not merely in private silence.

options.text: With David withdrawing from public worship.
options.note: The verse describes the opposite, public praise in the congregations.

questions: David invites God to test and examine his heart rather than avoiding scrutiny. What part of your life do you tend to keep from God's honest examination?
David deliberately chooses not to sit with deceitful or wicked company. What relationships or environments in your life may be quietly shaping you away from integrity?

David says he loves the house where God dwells and the place where His glory resides. What has your own posture toward corporate worship revealed about your love, or lack of love, for God's presence among His people?

David asks not to be swept away with sinners even though he has walked apart from their schemes. Where do you find yourself needing to trust God's justice rather than anxiously trying to control outcomes?
The psalm closes with resolve to bless the LORD publicly in the congregation. What would it look like for you to praise God more openly among others this week, not only in private?

translationNotes.note: Integrity renders tom, wholeness or sincerity of character, not sinless perfection but a settled, undivided loyalty to God.
Test and try both translate verbs used elsewhere of refining metal, picturing God's examination as a purifying process rather than a hostile interrogation.
Washing hands in innocence was a ritual gesture of approaching worship with a clear conscience, later echoed in the language of hearts and bodies washed clean in Hebrews 10:22.
